paragraphs.text: PREFACE.
Eucherius to Veranus, his son in Christ, greeting.

Out of the zeal of my fatherly concern for you, I thought I should compose and send you these formulas of spiritual understanding, so that once you have grasped them, a docile mind might readily apply itself to understanding all the divine writings. For since the letter kills but the spirit gives life, we must, by the life-giving Spirit, penetrate to the inner meaning of spiritual words. Moreover, that the whole of Scripture, of the Old Instrument as well as of the New, is to be taken in an allegorical sense, we are reminded both by what we read in the Old Testament: "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter ancient riddles," and by what is written in the New Testament: "All these things Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them." Nor should it be surprising that the divine word, uttered by the mouths of prophets and apostles, has departed far from the customary way in which men write, keeping easy things ready at hand while containing great things in its depths. For it was truly fitting that the sacred sayings of God should be distinguished from other writings in appearance as well as in merit, so that the dignity of heavenly mysteries should not lie open everywhere and indiscriminately to all, setting what is holy before dogs and pearls before swine; and so that, truly after the manner of that dove covered with silver, whose hinder parts shine with the look of gleaming gold, the first things in divine Scripture should gleam with silver while the more hidden things glow red with gold. Rightly, then, was it arranged that the chastity of the sacred utterances should be covered from the indiscriminate gaze of all by its own concealment, as by a kind of veil of modesty; and divine dispensation excellently provided that the writings themselves should be thus covered, overshadowed by heavenly mysteries, just as the Godhead itself was hidden in its own secrecy. Therefore, since in the holy books we find written the eyes of the Lord, the womb of the Lord, his feet, and even the weapons of the Lord, and since it is far from the catholic faith of the churches that God, who is invisible, incomprehensible, unchangeable and infinite, should be bounded by a body, we must inquire how these things are unlocked by the Holy Spirit through figurative interpretation. For here are found the inner chambers of the Lord's temple; here is the holy of holies. The body of sacred Scripture, then, as tradition has it, lies in the letter; its soul in the moral sense, which is called tropical; its spirit in the higher understanding, which is called anagoge. This threefold rule of the Scriptures fittingly accords with the confession of the Trinity, which sanctifies us in all things, so that our spirit and soul and body may be kept whole and blameless for the coming and the judgment of our Lord God Jesus Christ. The wisdom of this world divided its philosophy into three parts: physics, ethics and logic, that is, natural, moral and rational philosophy. The natural pertains to the causes of nature, which embraces all things; the moral looks to conduct; and the rational, disputing about higher things, affirms that God is the Father of all. Not far removed from this threefold division of teaching is the distinction our own writers make in their discussions, by which all the learned think that this heavenly philosophy of the Scriptures should be expounded according to history, according to tropology, and according to anagoge. Accordingly, history impresses upon us the truth of events and the trustworthiness of the account; tropology applies mystical meanings to the amendment of life; anagoge leads us up to the more sacred secrets of heavenly figures. There are also those who think that allegory should be added in fourth place in this kind of knowledge, and they affirm that through the narration of deeds it has held out a foreshadowing of things to come. To make these things clearer by examples: heaven, according to history, is this which we behold; according to tropology, the heavenly life. Waters, according to allegory, are baptism; according to anagoge, the angels; hence that saying: "And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord." Now the whole discipline of our religion has flowed from a twofold source of knowledge, the first of which they called practice and the second theoretice, that is, active and contemplative: the one brings the active life to perfection through the amendment of conduct, the other is occupied with the contemplation of heavenly things and the discussion of the divine Scriptures. Active knowledge, then, spreads out into various pursuits, while contemplative knowledge branches into two parts: it consists in historical discussion and in the interpretation of spiritual understanding. But setting these matters aside for now, let us set forth the formulas of spiritual understanding that we promised, running through the figures of individual names according to the senses in which they are usually to be taken where they occur in the text of the divine reading. Let us therefore pray the Lord to reveal the thickets of his Scriptures, and let us set out how they are to be understood in a more hidden sense:
I. On the things that are called members of the Lord, or that signify him,
II. On the creatures above,
III. On earthly things,
IV. On living creatures,
V. On various names and designations,
VI. On the inner man,
VII. On things in common use and in everyday life,
VIII. On the various meanings of words and names,
IX. On Jerusalem and her adversaries,
X. On numbers.
Now, then, as the gift of the Lord may suggest, let us explain the meanings of the names and words themselves, according to which they are chiefly drawn into allegory.
I. ON THE THINGS THAT ARE CALLED MEMBERS OF THE LORD, OR THAT SIGNIFY HIM.
The eyes of the Lord are understood as God's watchful regard; in the Psalm: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous."
The ears of the Lord: when he deigns to hear; in the Psalm: "and his ears are open to their prayers."
The mouth of the Lord: his speech to men; in the Prophet: "The mouth of the Lord has spoken."
The Word of the Lord: the Son; in the Psalm: "My heart has poured forth a good word."
The arm of the Lord: the Son, through whom he made all things; in the Prophet: "To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?"
The right hand of the Lord: the same as above; in the Psalm: "The right hand of the Lord has done mightily."
The womb of the Lord: the hidden depth from which he brought forth the Son; in the Psalm: "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you."
The feet of the Lord: the steadfastness of eternity; in the Psalm: "and darkness was under his feet."
The footprints of the Lord: the signs of his hidden works; in the Psalm: "and your footprints will not be known."
The steps of the Lord: the coming or visitation of the Lord; in the Psalm: "Your steps have been seen, O God."
The weapons of the Lord: his help given to the saints; in the Psalm: "Take hold of arms and shield."
The shield: God's protection; in the Psalm: "Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will."
The spear: divine vengeance; in the Psalm: "Draw out the spear and close in upon the ungodly."
The bow: the intent of God's threatening; in the Psalm: "He has bent his bow and made it ready."
Arrows: the divine commandments, or the apostles; in the Psalm: "He sent forth his arrows and scattered them."
The sword: vengeance, or the word of the Lord; in the Apostle: "For the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword."
The broadsword: the same as above.
The trumpet of God: the manifest voice of the Lord; in the Apostle: "at the command, and at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God."
The chariot of God: the seat of God, or the fourfold form of the Gospels; in the Psalm: "The chariot of God is ten thousandfold."
The rod of God: a sign of kingship, or the correction of discipline; in the Psalm: "A rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom."
The staff of God: the support of God's consolation; in the Psalm: "Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me."
Coals of fire: of love, or of examples, or of penance; in the Psalm: "with desolating coals."

Smoke: the beginnings of compunction to come, or of God's threatening itself; in the Psalm: "Smoke went up in his wrath." Again, in another sense, it is like smoke harmful to the eyes, that is, vanity.
Fire: the Holy Spirit; in the Acts of the Apostles: "And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit."
II. ON THE CREATURES ABOVE.
The heavens: the apostles or the saints, because the Lord dwells in them; in the Psalm: "The heavens declare the glory of God."
Clouds: the prophets or the saints, because they rain down the word of the Lord; in Isaiah: "I will command the clouds not to rain upon it."
Thunders: the voices of the Gospel, because they thunder from heaven; in the Psalm: "The voice of thunder in the wheel."
Flashes of lightning: the splendours of the Gospel; in the Psalm: "Your lightnings lit up the world."
Lightnings: the mighty works or the words of Jesus Christ; in the Psalm: "and he multiplied lightnings and threw them into confusion."
Thrones: angels or saints, or the very power of reigning; in the Psalm: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever." Again, in another sense, of the devil: "I will set my throne in the north."
Seats: the same as above, angels or saints, because the Lord sits in them; in the Psalm: "God sits upon his holy seat."
The sun: the Lord Jesus Christ, because he shines upon the earth; in Solomon: "So the sun of righteousness did not shine upon us."
The moon: the Church, because she shines in the night of this world; in the Psalm: "He made the moon for the seasons."
Stars: the saints or the learned; in Daniel: "The learned shall shine like stars"; sometimes also the angels.
Mist: the veil of God's mysteries; in the Prophet: "and the clouds are the dust of his feet."
Darkness: the covering of divine secrets; in the Psalm: "and darkness was under his feet."
The abyss: the depth of the Scriptures; in the Psalm: "Deep calls to deep."
Dew: the word of the Lord, because it moistens the earth of men; in the Psalm: "like the dew of Hermon, which comes down upon Mount Zion."
Rain: the precepts or commandments of the Lord, because it waters the earth, that is, men; in the Psalm: "A willing rain, O God, you will set apart for your inheritance."
Snow: chiefly for the whiteness of righteousness; in the Psalm: "You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
Hail: the threats of the Lord, with which he beats down the stubborn; in the Psalm: "hail and coals of fire." Again, in another sense: "and he killed their vines with hail."
Frost: abstinence, because through it the heat of the body grows cold; in the Psalm: "I have become like a wineskin in the frost."
Tempest: the onslaught of persecutions or tribulations; in the Psalm: "who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the tempest."
Ice: the hardness of sins; in Solomon: "and as ice in fair weather, so shall your sins melt away."
Winds: the souls of the saints; in the Psalm: "He flew upon the wings of the winds." Again, in a bad sense, in Matthew: "and the winds blew."
The north wind: the devil, or unbelieving or wicked men; in the Prophet: "From the north evils shall blaze forth upon the earth."

The right-hand wind: the same as above; in Solomon: "The north wind is a harsh wind." It is called by the name "right-hand" because the devil presumes to take for himself the name of "right," as though he were good, or because it is on the right hand of those who face the west, that is, sin. The south wind: the warmth of faith; in the Psalm: "like a torrent in the south."
Air: the utterance of emptiness; in the Apostle: "So I fight, not as one beating the air," that is, not chasing after empty things.
Seasons: the timely dispensation of the divine will; in the Psalm: "He made the moon for the seasons."
Spring: the renewal of life, whether through baptism or through the resurrection; in the Psalm: "Summer and spring, you made them."
Summer: a foreshadowing of the joy to come; in the Psalm, the same as above.
Winter: persecution or tribulation; in the Gospel: "that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath."
Years are sometimes taken for eternity, as here: "Your years shall not fail"; and sometimes for the shortness of life, as here: "Our years shall be reckoned as a spider's web."
Day and night: righteousness and wickedness, faith and unbelief, prosperity and adversity; in the Psalm: "By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he made it known."
Light and darkness are taken chiefly in the same way as day and night; in the epistle of John: "He who loves his brother abides in the light, but he who hates his brother is in darkness."
Shadow: divine protection; in the Psalm: "Protect me under the shadow of your wings."
An hour: five hundred years, as some think, whenever a day is taken for the whole age of this world; in the epistle of John: "Little children, it is the last hour."
The rising sun: chiefly the Saviour; in Luke: "The rising sun from on high has visited us"; and in Zechariah: "Behold a man whose name is the Rising."
The setting sun: the failing of the better life; in the Prophet: "The sun shall set for you at noon."
Morning: the light of good deeds, or baptism, or the resurrection; in the Psalm: "In the morning I will stand before you and see you."
Noon: the full brightness of teachings and deeds; in Solomon: "Where do you lie down at noon?" And in a bad sense, in the Psalm: "from the noonday demon," that is, the one that is out in the open.
Evening: the end of life or of the world, or punishment; in the Psalm: "Weeping will linger in the evening, and joy in the morning."
III. ON EARTHLY THINGS.
Earth: man himself; in the Gospel: "Other seed fell on good earth." Again, in a bad sense, of the sinner: "Earth you shall eat all the days of your life."
Dry land: the flesh of the fruitless man; in Ecclesiasticus: "to cover the dry land with malice and deceit."
Dust: sinners, or the vanity of the flesh; in the Psalm: "like the dust which the wind drives away."
Clay: the glue of sins; in the Psalm: "Rescue me out of the clay, that I may not stick fast." Again, in another sense, in John: "He made clay and anointed my eyes."

Mountains: the Lord, the Church, the apostles or the saints, from the loftiness of their virtues; in the Psalm: "which comes down upon Mount Zion." Again, in another sense, in the Prophet: "lest your feet stumble upon the dark mountains," that is, the heretics.
Hills: saints, but of lesser merit; in the Psalm: "mountains and all hills." Again, in a bad sense, in the Gospel: "Every hill and mountain shall be brought low."
Valleys: those made humble by contrition of heart; in the Psalm: "and the valleys shall abound with grain." And in a bad sense, the Prophet: "the valley of the sons of Hinnom."
The rock: Christ, from his firmness; in the Apostle: "and the rock was Christ."
Stones: sometimes Christ, or the saints; in the Psalm: "The stone which the builders rejected." Again, in another sense: "God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham."
The field: this world; in the Gospel: "The field is this world."
Plains: the saints or the divine Scriptures, because they provide pasture for souls; in the Psalm: "and your plains shall be filled with abundance." Again, in a bad sense: "in the plain of Tanis."
Pastures: spiritual refreshment; in the Psalm: "In a place of pasture, there he has set me."
Tilled land: the saints, who are cultivated for God; the Apostle: "You are God's tillage."
The husbandman: God; in the Gospel the Lord says: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman."
Furrows: the hearts of the saints; in the Psalm: "drenching its furrows."
Seed: divine preaching; in the Gospel: "The sower went out to sow his seed."

The harvest: the abundance or multitude of the faithful; in the Gospel: "Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for the harvest." And otherwise: "The harvest is the end of the world, and the reapers are the angels." Sheaves: the fruits of righteousness; in the Psalm: "carrying their sheaves."

Stubble: those who are dry toward the faith, or the empty; in the Apostle: "wood, hay, stubble"; and in the Prophet: "Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest," that is: I have found no fruits of good works.
The threshing floor: the Church; in the Gospel: "and he will thoroughly clear his threshing floor."
The winnowing fan: the testing of God's justice; in the Gospel: "whose winnowing fan is in his hand."
Wheat: the saints, or the elect of God; in the Gospel: "and he will gather his wheat into the barn."
Barley: the letter of the law; in the Gospel: "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves."
Chaff: sinners; in the Gospel: "but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire"; and Jeremiah: "What has the chaff to do with the wheat? says the Lord."
Tares: stumbling blocks, or those who live wickedly; in the Gospel: "His enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat."
The vineyard: the Church, or the people of Israel; in the Psalm: "You brought a vineyard out of Egypt." Again, in a bad sense: "For their vine is from the vineyard of Sodom."
The vine: Christ; in the Gospel: "I am the true vine." Again, in another sense, as above, in the Song of Deuteronomy: "Their vine is from the vineyard of Sodom."
Branches: the apostles or the saints; in the Gospel: "I am the vine, you are the branches." And in a bad sense, in the Song of Deuteronomy: "and their branch is from Gomorrah."
Grapes: the fruits of righteousness; in the Song of Isaiah: "I waited for it to bring forth grapes." Again, in a bad sense, in Deuteronomy: "their grapes are grapes of gall."
The cluster: the Church, or the body of the Lord; in Numbers: "because the children of Israel had carried a cluster from there."

The vintage: the end of the world, or vengeance upon a people; in the Psalm: "All who pass along the way pick its grapes." And Joel: "Put in the sickles and [?] the vineyard of the earth, for its grapes are ripe."

The winepress: the altar, because offerings are brought there like fruits; in the Song of Isaiah: "and I dug a winepress in it." And otherwise the winepress is the pressure of tribulations, in which the faithful are proved; in the title of a psalm: "To the end, for the winepresses."
Grass: the flesh, or vainglory; in the Prophet: "All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass."
Green plants: a certain delight of the soul that is making progress; in Genesis: "Let the earth bring forth green plants." Again, in a bad sense: "In the morning let it pass away like grass."
Flowers: Christ, or the beauty of righteousness; in the Psalm: "The righteous will flourish like the palm."
The lily: Christ or the angels, from the whiteness of righteousness; in Solomon: "I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys."
Roses: the martyrs, from the redness of their blood; in Solomon: "like a rose growing beside moist streams."
Violets: the confessors, because of their likeness to bruised bodies; in the Song of Songs: "Flowers have appeared on the earth."

Forests: the nations; in the Psalm: "We found it in the fields of the forest." From these forests came out the two bears, the kings of the Romans, at the command of the figurative Elisha, and forty-two years after his ascension into heaven they devoured the Jewish boys.
Thickets: the dark or covered places of the divine Scriptures; in the Psalm: "and he will reveal the thickets."
Wood: sinners destined for the fire; in Ecclesiastes: "He who splits wood will be endangered by it." Again, in a good sense: "And he shall be like a tree that is planted."
The root: origin; in the Apostle: "If the root is holy, so are the branches." And in a bad sense, in the Psalm: "and your root from the land of the living."

The tree: man, from the fruit of his works; in the Gospel: "Either make the tree good and its fruit good." And in a bad sense: "or make the tree bad and its fruit bad." Some think that in this text the tree should be taken as man's will rather than as man himself.
The branch: succession; in the Apostle: "If the root is holy, so are the branches." Again, in a bad sense, in Daniel: "Cut off its branches."
The leaf: the word of teaching; in the Psalm: "and its leaf shall not fall." And otherwise the leaf is clothing and comeliness, together with the protection of divine grace.
Fruits: the fruit of the saints in virtues; in the Song of Songs: "and let him eat the fruit of his apple trees."
The palm: perfection or victory; in the Psalm: "The righteous will flourish like the palm."
Cedars: men of loftier power; in the Psalm: "Like the cedars of Lebanon they shall be multiplied." And in a bad sense, in the Psalm: "and the Lord will shatter the cedars of Lebanon."
The olive: the saint who abounds in the fruits of mercy; in the Psalm: "But I am like a fruitful olive tree."
The wild olive: a man without fruit, or a gentile; in the Apostle: "For if you were cut from the wild olive tree, which is yours by nature."
The fig tree: sometimes the synagogue; in the Gospel: "and at once the fig tree withered." And in Habakkuk: "The fig tree will not bear fruit."
Pomegranates: the Church gathered from many nations, or possessing diverse graces; in the Song of Songs: "Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, with the fruit of apples."

The reed: the sinner, or one who is weak in faith; in the Gospel: "A bruised reed he will not break." Again, the reed is feeble help; in the Prophet: "Why do you trust in this staff of Egyptian reed? If anyone leans on it, it will break and pierce his hand."

The bramble bush: as some think, a prefiguration of the holy Virgin Mary, because from the bramble, as it were, of a human body she brought forth the Saviour like a rose; or because she bore the force of the divine radiance without being consumed; in Exodus: "And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush, and he saw that the bush was burning and was not consumed."
Thorns: sometimes the harmful cares of riches that choke the mind; in the Gospel: "Other seed fell among thorns."
Thistles: the stings of vices or of temptations; in Genesis: "Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you."
Springs: baptism; in the Psalm: "As the deer longs for the springs of water."

Water: peoples, or temptations; in the Psalm: "Perhaps the water would have swallowed us up." Again, in a good sense, in Jeremiah: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." And in the Prophet: "You who thirst, come to the water," that is, to teaching.
The torrent: the onset of persecution; in the Psalm: "He will drink from the torrent by the way." And in a good sense: "and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your delight."
Rivers: the peoples of unbelievers; in the Psalm: "By the rivers of Babylon." Again, in a good sense: "Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water," that is, of spiritual grace.
The pit: hell; in the Psalm: "They laid me in the lowest pit," that is, in that place of hell in which sinners alone are held in penal custody.
The sea: the world, or peoples; in the Psalm: "This great and wide sea."
Fish: the saints; in the Gospel: "and they hauled in the net full of large fish." Again, in a bad sense: "but the bad they threw away."
Billows: temptations; in the Psalm: "All your heights and your billows have passed over me."
Waves: the same as above; in the Song: "The waves congealed in the midst of the sea."
Islands: either souls or the churches of God, which are battered by the various billows of temptation; in the Psalm: "Let the many islands rejoice."
The shore: the end of the world; in the Gospel: "and sitting down on the shore they gathered the good into vessels."
The sand of the sea: the countless multitudes of the nations; in Genesis: "and I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand on the seashore."
IV. ON ANIMALS
Birds: the saints, because in their hearts they fly up to higher things. In the Gospel: "and it put out great branches, so that the birds of the air could dwell beneath its shade."
The flight of the saints: being carried out of oneself into God, or understanding in the Scriptures. In the Psalm: "and I will fly away and be at rest."
Wings: the two Testaments. In Ezekiel: "each covered its body with two wings."
Feathers: the Scriptures. In the Psalm: "the feathers of a dove, covered with silver."

Nest: the Church, or the lofty rest of the saints. In the Psalm: "and the turtledove a nest for herself, where she may lay her young." In another sense, the nest is a good conscience. There the offspring of good thoughts are cherished and then brought forth as works, so that afterwards they are called children. In the Psalm: "your children like young olive shoots around your table."
Young birds: the saints, as in the Psalm above. And in a bad sense, in Solomon: "and let the young eagles devour him."

Eagles: the saints. In the Gospel: "wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather." And in a bad sense: "let the young eagles devour him." Ostrich: a heretic or a philosopher, because although it has what look like the wings of wisdom, it still does not fly. In Isaiah: "and it shall be a lair for dragons and a pasture for ostriches."
Pelican: Christ the Lord in his passion, or a holy man given to solitude. In the Psalm: "I have become like a pelican of the wilderness."

Raven: the blackness of a sinner or of a demon. In Solomon: "may the ravens of the valleys dig it out." In a good sense, in the Song of Songs, of the bridegroom: "his locks are like fir trees, black as ravens."
Partridge: the devil. In the prophet: "the partridge cried out; it gathered what it had not hatched."
Dove: the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel: "and I saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove." In another sense: "in Ephraim, a senseless dove without a heart."

Turtledove: the Holy Spirit, or a holy man, or spiritual understanding. In the Song of Songs: "the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land." But the Holy Spirit is called a dove when the exposition of holy Scripture is plain, and is understood as a turtledove when the Scriptures rise to lofty and obscure mysteries.
Kite: signifies, I think, someone rapacious or proud. In the Psalm, according to the Hebrew: "the fir tree is the kite's house."
Hawk: sometimes, I think, a saint who seizes the kingdom of God. In Job: "Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows its feathers?"
Night raven: Christ, or a holy man despised by unbelievers. In the Psalm: "I have become like a night raven in its dwelling."

Sparrow: sometimes the Lord, or a holy man. In the Psalm: "for the sparrow has found itself a home." There is also a sparrow in another sense, as when it is said to the saint: "Move off to the mountain like a sparrow."

Rooster: the Lord, I think, or a saint. In Solomon: "and the rooster walking gladly among the hens." And in Job: "Who gave the rooster understanding?" And in the other sense: "and I will have you carried off as a rooster is carried off."
Hen: wisdom, or the Church, or the soul. In the Gospel: "as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings."
Bats: the monstrous idols given over to darkness. In the prophet: "so that you might worship moles and bats."
Beetle: in the prophet, "and the beetle shall cry out from the wood," which some think refers to the Lord.
Locusts: the peoples. In the Gospel: "and his food was locusts."
Bees: a figure of virginity or of wisdom. In Solomon: "go to the bee and learn what a worker she is." And in a bad sense, in the prophet: "and for the bee that is in Assyria."
Fly: the devil. In Solomon: "dying flies spoil the sweet ointment."
Beasts: the devil, or all savage men. In the Psalm: "do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess you."
Lion: the Lord: "the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered." In another sense: "lest he seize my soul like a lion."
Leopard: the devil, or a sinner of varied conduct. In the prophet: "as the Ethiopian will not change his skin, nor the leopard his spots."
Elephant: a monstrous sinner. In Kings: "and they brought apes and elephants to Solomon."
Bear: the devil, or cruel leaders. In Kings: "and two bears came out and devoured them."
Hart: Christ, or the saints: "as the hart longs for the springs of water."
Wolf: the devil, or heretics. In the Gospel: "but inwardly they are ravening wolves." In a good sense: "Benjamin is a ravening wolf," which signifies the apostle Paul.
Boar: the devil. In the Psalm: "the boar from the forest has laid it waste."
Tiger: sometimes womanish arrogance. In the book of Job, according to the Hebrew: "the tiger perished because it had no prey."
Rhinoceros: any strong person, in either a good or a bad sense. In the book of Job, according to the Hebrew: "Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?"

Monoceros, that is, the unicorn. In the Psalm: "and the beloved like the son of unicorns," that is, of singular power, or of the saints, who hold to the one Word of God. And in another sense: "and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns." Here the unicorns are the proud, or those who hold to only one Testament.

Wild ass: a hermit. In Job: "Who will let the wild ass go free?" The Jewish people can also be called a wild ass, because the same book goes on: "and who has loosed its bonds?", meaning, of course, the bonds of the commandments.
Fawn: Christ, or a saint, because of the variety of his graces. In Solomon: "be like a young doe, my kinsman, or a fawn of the harts."
Doe: the same as above.
Hare: one who fears God. In the Psalm: "the rock is a refuge for hares and hedgehogs."
Hedgehog: the same as above. And: "the hedgehogs, a feeble folk, who made their homes in the rocks."
Fox: a heretic, or the devil, or a crafty sinner. In the Gospel: "go and tell that fox."
Animal: the carnal man. In the Apostle: "but the animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God."
Beast of burden: one who lacks understanding and speech. In the Psalm: "I have become like a beast of burden before you."

Horse: a holy man. In Habakkuk: "you who mount your horses." And in a bad sense: "a horse is a false hope for safety." Mule: anyone without reason. In the Psalm: "do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding."
Ass: the human body, or the gentile people. In the Gospel: "and they brought the ass and her colt to Jesus and set him on them."
She-ass: [?], or a people lacking knowledge of God. In the Gospel, the same as above.

Camel: the rich, loaded with the things of this world, or people of twisted character. In the Gospel: "it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." Bulls: the princes of the peoples. In the Psalm: "fat bulls have besieged me."
Oxen: the apostles, who took up the yoke of Christ's Gospel and ploughed the world with the ploughshare. In the Psalm: "I will offer you oxen with goats."
Cows: those full of carnal vices. In the Psalm: "among the cows of the peoples."
Calf: Christ, or the saints: "then they shall lay calves upon your altar." And in another sense: "many calves have surrounded me," that is, wanton ones.
Swine: unclean sinners. In the epistle of Peter: "and the sow, once washed, back to wallowing in the mire."
Rams: the apostles, or the leaders of the churches. In the Psalm: "bring to the Lord the offspring of rams."
Sheep: the faithful peoples. In the Gospel: "my sheep hear my voice."
Flocks: the simpler sort, less endowed with subtlety of reasoning. In Solomon: "tend the souls of your flocks."
He-goats: sinners, or the gentiles. In Daniel: "and behold, a he-goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth." In a good sense: "I will offer you oxen with goats."
She-goats: the righteous, sometimes those coming from among the gentiles. In Solomon: "your hair is like a flock of goats that have come down from Gilead."
Lambs: Christ, or the apostles, or the saints. In the Gospel: "feed my lambs."
Kids: sinners. In the Gospel: "but the kids on the left." Moles: idols, or heretics, who do not see the truth. In Isaiah: "so that you might worship moles and bats."

Dog: the devil, or a Jew, or a gentile. In the Psalm: "and my only one from the power of the dog." And in another sense, in Ecclesiastes: "a living dog is better than a dead lion." Here they think the lion should be taken as the devil and the dog as a gentile or a sinful man, because the one can come to faith or repentance, while the other will not.

Frogs: demons. In the Apocalypse: "and I saw coming from the mouth of the dragon three unclean spirits like frogs; for they are spirits of demons." Frogs are also heretics, who linger in the slime of the vilest notions and never stop babbling their empty chatter.
Ant: one who is provident or hardworking. In Solomon: "go to the ant, you sluggard."

Worm: Christ, because of the lowliness of the humanity he took on. In the Psalm: "but I am a worm and no man." In another sense, in Isaiah: "their worm shall not die," meaning either the worm itself or the conscience of sin.
Spider: human frailty. In the Psalm: "and you made his soul waste away like a spider."
Serpent: the devil, or wicked men. In the Gospel: "you serpents, brood of vipers." In the other sense, in the Gospel: "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert."
Dragon: the devil, or an open persecutor. In the Psalm: "you crushed the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the people of the Ethiopians."
Scorpion: the devil, or his ministers. In the Gospel: "I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions."
Viper: the same as above. In the Gospel: "you serpents, brood of vipers."
V. ON VARIOUS NAMES AND TITLES

Man: either the whole man or the mind. In Genesis: "God made man in his own image and likeness." And in a bad sense, in the Psalm: "Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail," that is, the flesh or the devil.

Husband: the spirit, that is, the mind. In the Apostle: "the head of the woman is the man." In a bad sense, in Genesis: "a very beautiful virgin, whom no man had known." Here the man is the devil, who often corrupts the mind through its thoughts.
Woman: the soul, or human flesh. In the Apostle: "the head of the woman is the man."
Virgin: the Church, or holy souls. In the Apostle: "for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ."
King: the Lord. In the Apostle: "King of kings and Lord of lords."
Queen: the Church. In the Psalm: "the queen stood at your right hand." The queen is also the soul ruling the body.
Father: the Lord. In the prophet: "and I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty."
Mother: the Church, or the heavenly Jerusalem. In the Apostle: "but the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother."
Brother: Christ, or one's neighbor. In the Psalm: "I will declare your name to my brothers."
Sister: the Church as sister to the synagogue, or the soul as sister to Christ. In the Song of Songs: "my sister, my bride."
Husband and wife: Christ and the Church; also the spiritual understanding and the historical sense of the Scriptures. In the Apostle: "husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church."
Bridegroom: Christ, because he was pledged by the Father from the beginning. In the Psalm: "and he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber."
Bride: the Church, which was promised through divine pledges. In the Song of Songs: "come from Lebanon, my bride, come from Lebanon."
Son: the people of believers. In the Apostle: "you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God."
Daughter: the faithful soul, or the Church. In the Psalm: "listen, daughter, and see."
Neighbors: those near in faith. In Solomon: "come, eat and drink and be drunk, my neighbors."
Friends: those of one mind in God. In the Gospel: "you are my friends."

Old man: one of perfected righteousness. In Genesis: "and Abraham died, an old man and full of days." And in Solomon: "understanding is a man's gray hair, and a spotless life is his old age." And in the other sense, of Solomon: "and when he was already old, his heart was led astray."

Young men: those eager for God. In the epistle of John: "I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one." And in a bad sense, in the book of Kings, of Rehoboam: "forsaking the counsel of the elders, he spoke according to the counsel of the young men."

Little child: one humble and simple in mind. In the Gospel: "you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little children." In the other sense, in the Apostle: "when I was a child, I spoke like a child."
Harlot: the sinful soul, which has left its heavenly husband, that is, Christ, and conceives from the devil the adulterous fruits of iniquity. In Jeremiah: "you have taken on the face of a harlot."
Laborers: the apostles, or the preachers of the Gospel. In the Gospel: "the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few."
Shepherd: the Lord: "I am the good shepherd." The shepherd is also the apostle. In the Gospel: "feed my sheep."
Hired servants: those who serve the Lord not out of love for God alone but for a temporal reward. In the Gospel: "how many of my father's hired servants have bread in plenty!"
Fishermen: the apostles, or teachers. In the Gospel: "and I will make you fishers of men."
Physician: Christ, or a learned man. In Solomon: "a gentle man is the physician of the heart." And again: "those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick."

Rich man: the believer abounding in spiritual goods. In the Apostle: "for in him you have been made rich in all knowledge and in all speech." And in a bad sense, in the Gospel: "woe to you who are rich." Poor man: the humble. In the Gospel: "and there was a certain poor man named Lazarus." And again: "blessed are the poor in spirit." In a bad sense, in the Psalm: "for we have become exceedingly poor."
Clothed: one who keeps the integrity of baptism or of faith. In the Gospel: "and he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment."

Naked: one who lacks the garment of baptism or divine help. In the Apocalypse: "but you are naked and wretched." And in a good sense, in the Gospel: "and leaving the linen cloth behind, he fled from them naked," that is, naked of earthly possessions.
The living: the righteous. In the Psalm: "I will please the Lord in the land of the living." And in the other sense, in Ecclesiastes: "and I praised the dead more than the living."

The dead: sinners, or unbelievers. In the Gospel: "let the dead bury their own dead." And in a good sense: "blessed are the dead who die in the Lord." And also: "you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God."
Corpses: the bodies of unbelievers. In the prophet: "and I will fill the valley of Jehoshaphat with the corpses of the dead." In another sense: "they have laid out the corpses of your servants."

Tomb: the body of a sinner, which holds within it a soul dead through vices. In the Gospel: "for you are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful to people on the outside, but inside are full of dead men's bones."
VI. ON THE INNER MAN
The inner man: the rational soul. In the Apostle: "that Christ may dwell in the inner man through faith in your hearts."

His head: Christ. In the Apostle: "the head of man is Christ." Crown of the head: the summit of righteousness. In Solomon: "for your head shall receive a crown of graces." In a bad sense: "the hairy crown of those who go about in their pleasures," that is, the height of wickedness.
Hair: the adornment of righteousness, or the senses. In the Gospel: "but even the hairs of your head are all numbered."
Eyes: faithful and simple understanding. In the Gospel: "but blessed are your eyes, for they see." And in a bad sense, in the Gospel: "if your eye is evil."
Ears: faithful obedience. In the Gospel: "and your ears, for they hear."
Nostrils: the breath of faith and of good virtues. In Job: "and the divine spirit is in my nostrils." And in a bad sense, in Job: "smoke comes out of his nostrils," that is, the devil's.
Throat: the judgment of the understanding. In the book of Job: "and does not my throat meditate wisdom?" And in a bad sense: "my throat has grown hoarse."
Mouth: speech itself. In the Psalm: "the mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom."
Tongue: the same as above. In the Psalm: "and his tongue will speak justice."
Hand: work. In the Psalm: "and I washed my hands among the innocent."
Right hand: good works. In the Gospel: "do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing."

Left hand: works that are not good. In the Gospel, the same as above. Breast: the hidden depths of understanding. In the Gospel: "and the disciple whom Jesus loved most was reclining on the Lord's breast."
Belly: the capacity of reason. In Habakkuk: "my belly was troubled within me."
Kidneys: the innermost feelings. In the Psalm: "moreover, even into the night my kidneys have instructed me."
Loins: strength of mind. In the Apostle: "gird up the loins of your mind."
Navel: the craving of lust. In Job: "and his strength is in the navel of his belly," that is, because this signifies the genitals of women, just as the loins do those of men.
Fat: the richness of divine grace. In the Psalm: "let my soul be filled as with fat and richness." In a bad sense, fat is the grossness of malice. In the Psalm: "they have closed up their fat."
Bones: the firmness of the soul. In the Psalm: "all my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?" And in a bad sense, in the book of Job: "his bones are like pipes of bronze."

Bowels: the feeling of tenderness and mercy. In the Apostle: "if there are any bowels of compassion and mercy." And in the other sense, in the Acts of the Apostles, of Judas: "and his bowels gushed out."
Skins: a sign of mortality. In Genesis: "and he made them garments of skins."
Blood: the working of the flesh. In the Psalm: "deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation." And again: "flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God."
Flesh: the outer man. In the Apostle: "for the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh."

Knees: the confession of humility. In the canticle: "and now I bend the knees of my heart." Sometimes the strength of faith. In the prophet: "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."

Feet: the course of life, or the steadiness of the mind or of faith. In the Psalm: "our feet were standing." And in a bad sense, in the prophet: "why do you limp on both feet?" And: "their feet are swift to shed blood."
Heel: the overthrowing of vices. In Genesis: "he will watch for your head, and you for his heel." And in a bad sense: "he has lifted up his heel against me."
Steps: progress in good works. In the Psalm: "make my steps perfect in your paths."

Footprints: the marks of virtues. In the Psalm: "that my footprints may not be moved." And in the other sense, in Solomon: "and our life," that is, the life of the wicked, "has passed away like the track of a ship."
Robe: the garment of baptism or of faith. In the Gospel: "quickly, bring out the best robe."
Sackcloth: the witness of repentance. In the Gospel: "they would have repented long ago in ashes and sackcloth."
Girdle: being girded for spiritual work. In the Psalm: "and you have girded me with gladness."
Shoes: the preparation of peace. In the Apostle: "your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace."

The armor of the inner man. In the Apostle: "having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God."
VII. On things that are in common use and ready to hand.
Bread: Christ, or the word of the Lord. In the Gospel: "I am the living bread."
Wine: the same as above. In Solomon: "And drink the wine that I have mixed for you."
Oil: mercy, or the Holy Spirit. In the psalm: "With my holy oil I have anointed him." In the opposite sense: "But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head", that is, flattery.
Pork: sins. In the psalm: "They are glutted with pork."
Unleavened: free of the leaven of malice. In the Apostle: "With the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."
Fine flour: purity of mind and strength of love. In Leviticus: "If a soul offers a gift in sacrifice to God, let its gift be fine flour."
Cakes baked in the ashes: the offering of humility. In Genesis: "Quickly knead three measures of fine flour and make cakes in the ashes."

Milk: sincerity of mind. In the Epistle of Peter: "Long for the spiritual milk without guile." In another sense: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it." Here milk means a slender understanding.
Curdled: hardened by vices. In the psalm: "Their heart is curdled like milk."
Salt: the seasoning of wisdom. In the Gospel: "You are the salt of the earth."

Honey: the sweetness of God's commandments. In the psalm: "How sweet are your words to my palate, Lord, sweeter than honey to my mouth." In another sense, in Solomon: "When you find honey, eat as much as is enough, lest you be filled with it and vomit it up", that is, do not seek after things too high for you.
Gall: the bitterness of malice. In the psalm: "They gave me gall for my food."
Vinegar: the harshness of a corrupt mind. In the psalm: "And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink."
Pitch: the defilement and blackness of sins. In Solomon: "Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it."
Strong drink: a kind of concoction of wickedness. In the Gospel: "He shall drink no wine or strong drink."
The Lord's cup: his passion. In the psalm: "I will take the cup of salvation."
Unmixed wine: the purity of judgement or of truth, or the warmth of faith. In the psalm: "It is full of unmixed wine, mingled."
Dregs: the last of the judgement. In the psalm: "Yet its dregs have not been emptied out."
Food: the word or will of the Lord. In the Gospel: "My food is to do the will of the Father who sent me."
Drink: the same as above. In the psalm: "And you will give them drink from the torrent of your will", that is, from the Holy Spirit. In another sense: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink."
Storehouses: the inner chambers of the heart. In the song of Deuteronomy: "And in the storehouses, terror."
Bag: anxiety about one's livelihood. In the Gospel: "No bag for the journey."
Purse: laying up treasure with God. In the Gospel: "Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old." And in another sense: "Let us all have one common purse", that is, avarice.
Money: the divine words. In the Gospel: "You ought therefore to have put my money with the bankers."
Fleece: the people. In the psalm: "And he will come down like rain upon the fleece."
Linen: spiritual strength or brightness. In Exodus: "And for the sons of Aaron you shall prepare linen tunics."
Wineskins: the vessels of the human body. In the Gospel: "New wine must be put into new wineskins."
Flour: good works, or knowledge. In the Gospel: "A woman hid it in three measures of flour."

Mill: the conversion of life. In the Gospel: "Two women grinding at the mill." The millstones can also signify the two Testaments, by which, through the labour of those who expound them, the wheat of the Old Testament is turned into the flour of the Gospel.

These names, then, when they occur in the text of sacred Scripture, are handed down to be understood in this way, or above all in the plainer senses we have set out, although they mostly pass into various meanings according to person, time or place, and break forth into figures suited to their contexts, as the logic of allegorical interpretation requires. Thus, for example,

the abyss is understood, as we said above, as the depth of the Scriptures; and the abyss is also the immensity of the waters: "And the fountains of the great deep burst open." The abyss is also the unspeakable judgements of God: "Your judgements are a great deep." The abyss is also hell: "Or who will descend into the abyss?", that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. The abyss is also human hearts darkened by crimes: "The abyss said, It is not in me", that is, wisdom.

Fire, as we mentioned above, is taken to mean the Holy Spirit. Fire is also love: [?] its enclosure, the fire of its flames. Fire is tribulation: "You have tried us with fire, as silver is tried by fire." Fire is wrath: "And I will consume them in the fire of my wrath, says the Lord." Fire is lust: "They are all adulterers; their hearts are like an oven."

Shadow, as we have shown, signifies divine protection; but shadow sometimes means sins: "Those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death." Shadow sometimes means punishments; in Job: "Where the shadow of death is, and no order." And just as a shadow is never far from the thing whose shadow it is, so death is not far from the punishment that brings death. Shadow is sometimes the delight of sinners; in Job, of the devil: "He sleeps under the shade, in the covert of the reed and in moist places." And there is again another kind, in which many things signify one thing.
We have mentioned that those two millstones can signify the two Testaments; and likewise the two Testaments are signified by the two

cherubim in Exodus; the two living creatures in Habakkuk; the two rocks in Exodus and in the Song of Songs, under whose cover Moses and the bride are sheltered; and the two bronze mountains in Zechariah, from whose myrtle thickets and dark shade come forth chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses.

But we have judged that to pursue such manifold meanings for every single name would be not only an immense labour but an impossible one. So now let us return to the method and order of interpretation that we interrupted for a little, as the discussion required.

Baskets: the apostles. In the Gospel: "And they took up what was left over, twelve baskets full of fragments." In another sense: "His hands served at the basket", that is, in the slavery or tribulation that the Egyptians imposed.
Chair: teaching. In the psalm: "And let them praise him in the chair of the elders." In the bad sense: "And has not sat in the chair of pestilence", that is, in the teaching of heretics.
Footstool: the subjection of the humbled. In the psalm: "Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet."
Balance: equity, or the power of divine government. In Isaiah: "And he weighed the mountains on scales and the hills in a balance."
Ashes: the emptiness of human frailty. In Solomon: "Why are earth and ashes proud?"

Pot: lineage. In the psalm: "Moab is the pot of my hope", that is, because Christ's lineage according to the flesh descended from Ruth the Moabitess. In another sense, a pot is the seething of tribulation; in the prophet: "And I saw a boiling pot, and its face was toward the north." Torches: souls shining with righteousness. In the Gospel: "And they trimmed their torches."
Lamp: the Church, or the soul. In the Gospel: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning." Sometimes lamps are good works: "Let your light so shine that they may see your good works."
Bushel: the human body, or the letter of the law, or the Jewish people. In the Gospel: "No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel."
Lampstand: the Church, or the body of the Lord, or holy Scripture. In the prophet: "And I saw two burning lampstands at the right of the altar."
Table: the altar, or spiritual refreshment. In the psalm: "You have prepared a table before me."

Keys: the opening up of spiritual knowledge. In Luke: "Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge: you did not go in yourselves, and you hindered those who were going in." Keys are also the virtues of justice, mercy and piety. In the Gospel: "To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven."
Bars: the barriers of the divine commandments against the wicked: "For he has strengthened the bars of your gates."
Hatchet: persecution by the wicked. In the psalm: "With double axe and hatchet they have brought it down."

Double axe: twofold affliction. In the psalm, the same as above. Ship: the Church. In the Gospel: "The boat was being tossed by many waves in the middle of the sea." A person, too, is often called a boat, so that the sailors may be understood as the thoughts that steer him.
Nets: preaching. In the Gospel: "And let down your nets for a catch."
Beam: a graver sin. In the Gospel: "First take the beam out of your own eye."
Speck: a lighter sin. In the Gospel: "And then you will see to take the speck out of your brother's eye."
Snare: deceit. In the psalm: "They have laid snares for my feet."

Cords: one's lot or inheritance. In the psalm: "The cords have fallen for me in pleasant places." Cords are also sins: "Woe to you who drag sins along like a long rope." And: "The cords of sinners have entangled me."
Wheel: the world, or human life. In the psalm: "The voice of thunder in the wheel." And again: "My God, make them like a wheel", that is, make them fickle and unstable in their wickedness.
Sponge: the hollow unbelief of the Jews. In the Gospel: "But they put a sponge full of vinegar on hyssop and held it to his mouth."
Ladder: the progress of the saints. In Genesis: "And in his sleep he saw a ladder standing on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it."
Brooms: the cares of superstition arising from vainglory. In the Gospel: "And when he comes, he finds it empty, swept with brooms and put in order."
Pearl: the teaching of the Gospel, or the hope of the kingdom of heaven. In the Gospel: "When he had found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it."
Ring: the seal of faith. In the Gospel: "And put a ring on his hand." Of this also in the psalm: "The light of your face, Lord, is sealed upon us."
Cloak: the adornment of praise. In Solomon: "She made cloaks for her husband", that is, a garment made, as it were, of the two Testaments.
Gold: the inner understanding of the Scriptures. In the psalm: "And the back of her shoulders with the look of gold."
Silver: the divine words, or the understanding of the letter or of the history. In the psalm: "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire."
Precious stones: the apostles or the saints, or the works of virtue themselves. In Revelation: "The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone."
Bronze: vanity, or emptiness of faith. In the Apostle: "I have become like sounding brass." In another sense: "You have made my arms like a bow of bronze." Here bronze means strong or firm.
Iron: tribulation, or the man himself. In the psalm: "Iron pierced his soul."
Lead: the weight of sins. In the prophet: "And I saw iniquity sitting upon a talent of lead."
Earthenware: the frailty of the flesh. In the Apostle: "We have this treasure in earthen vessels."
VIII. On the various meanings of verbs and nouns.
To build: to do good works, or to teach well. In the Apostle: "If anyone builds on this foundation gold, silver, precious stones."
To destroy: to practise evil works, or to teach badly. In Solomon: "One builds and another destroys."
To cleanse: to purge of vices. In the Gospel: "Jesus touched him, saying, I will it: be clean. And at once his leprosy was cleansed."
To stand: to be steadfast in faith. In the Apostle: "Stand firm in the faith." To walk: to make one's way to the Lord. In the psalm: "And I walked in a broad place."
To sit: to recover oneself humbly in God. In the Gospel: "But you, sit in the city."
To lie: to give way to vices or temptations. In the Gospel: "And he found her lying on the bed."
To run: to hasten in good works. In the Apostle: "So run that you may win."
To keep watch: to keep guard over the heart, or to rise again toward God. In the psalm: "From the morning watch until night."

To sleep: to rest with Christ through one's passing. In the psalm: "Shall he who sleeps not rise again?" In another sense, to sleep is to grow sluggish in the slumber of sins. In the Apostle: "Rise, you who sleep."
Ascent: progress toward God. In the psalm: "Ascents in his heart."
Descent: falling away from God. In the Gospel: "A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho."
Way: Christ. In the Gospel: "I am the way, the truth and the life." In another sense, the way is a person's life. In the psalm: "I declared my ways, and you heard me."
Wide: broadened by the allurements of vices. In the Gospel: "Broad is the gate and wide the way that leads to destruction."
Narrow: strict, or hard pressed by tribulations. In the Gospel: "How narrow is the gate and hard the way that leads to life."
Straight: ordered by God's commandments. In Isaiah: "Make his paths straight."
Crooked: straying from God's commandments. In Isaiah: "And the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places smooth ways."
Smooth: levelled by obedience to the commandments. In Isaiah, the same as above.
Rough: bristling with the harshness of disobedience. In Isaiah, the same as above.
On the right: on the side of righteousness. In the Gospel: "He set the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left."
On the left: on the side of unrighteousness. In the Gospel, the same as above.
Pit: deceit, or a fall into death. In the psalm: "They dug a pit before my face."
Well: the devil, or hell. In the psalm: "Nor let the well close its mouth over me." And in a good sense, in Genesis: "At the well of the oath", that is, the water of faith.
Health: soundness of mind. In the psalm: "I cried to you, and you healed me."
Sickness: the disease of vices. In the psalm: "Who heals all your sicknesses."
Leprosy: the defilement of sins. In the Gospel: "And at once his leprosy was cleansed."
IX. ON JERUSALEM AND ITS ADVERSARIES
Jerusalem: the Church, or the soul. In the Psalm: “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem.” Note that whatever applies to the Church in general can also be applied to the soul.
Zion: the same as above. In the Psalm: “Praise your God, O Zion.”
The sons of Zion: the sons of the Church. In the Psalm: “And let the sons of Zion rejoice in their king.”
The daughters of Jerusalem: the same as above.
The tabernacle: the Lord’s body, or the Church. In the Psalm: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun.”

The ark: the Lord’s flesh, or the hearts of the saints, filled with God. In the Psalm: “You and the ark of your holiness.” Again, the ark is the Church, within which those who are to be saved are shut in. In Genesis: “And Noah alone remained, and those who were with him in the ark.”

The two tablets of stone: in my view, they stand for the two Testaments, or for the two commandments of love of God and of neighbour. In Exodus: “And the Lord said to Moses: Cut out for yourself two tablets.”
The law: the divine commandments. In the Psalm: “The law of the Lord is spotless.”
The bond: the written agreement made between sinful man and the devil by the hand of iniquity. In the Apostle: “the bond of sin that stood against us.”
The covenant: the alliance of divine grace with man. In the Psalm: “I saw those who did not keep the covenant.”
The testament: the confirmation of the divine will. In the Prophet: “And I will confirm the testament over the house of Judah.”

The foreskin: the life of the Gentiles. In the Apostle: “Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised”; that is, anyone who comes to faith in Christ from among the Gentiles is not to be circumcised in the body.
Circumcision: the stripping away of vices. In the Apostle: “You were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping off of the body of the flesh.”
The horn: strength, or kingship. In Kings: “And he exalted the horn of his anointed.”

Purple: the appearance of martyrdom through blood. In Exodus: “Everyone who is willing at heart shall bring firstfruits to the Lord: gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, scarlet, spun thread and fine linen.”
Scarlet: the same as above, or the ardour of love, or a reminder of the cross. In Exodus, as above.
Fine linen: the whiteness of chastity or continence. In Exodus, the same as above.
Blue: the bruises of the confessors. In Exodus, the same as above.

The ephod: it signifies works, being worn on the shoulders. In Exodus: “And they made the ephod of gold and blue and purple and scarlet spun thread and twisted fine linen.” The breastpiece: the declaration of doctrine or of reason, worn on the breast. In
Exodus: “And they made the breastpiece of woven work, like the work of the ephod.”
The robe reaching to the feet: a more hidden and more perfect doctrine. In Exodus: “And they made the robe reaching to the feet beneath the ephod [?], woven work, all of blue.”

The gold plate on the forehead: the sign of the cross set above. In Exodus: “And they made the gold plate,” and further on, it says, “they wrote on it in engraved letters the seal of the holiness of the Lord,” that is, the Lord’s four-letter name. The temple: the body of the Lord, or of the saints. In the Apostle: “For you are the temple of the living God.”
The altar: the loftiness of faith. In the Psalm: “Then they will lay calves upon your altar.”
Sacrifice: the offering of righteousness. In the Psalm: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness.”
The whole burnt offering: faith set wholly on fire. In the Psalm: “I will offer you burnt offerings full of marrow.”
The victim: Christ, or a soul dedicated to God. In the Apostle: “an offering and a victim to God for a fragrant aroma.”
Myrrh: a sign of mortality. In the Psalm: “Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments.”
Ointment: the grace of Christ’s name poured out. In Solomon: “Your name is ointment poured out.”

The Holy of Holies: all the inner mysteries of God, or the kingdom of heaven. In the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For Jesus did not enter a holy place made with hands, a copy of the true one, but heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf.”
The Sabbath: spiritual rest. In Genesis: “And the Lord rested from all his works.”
The forty days: a figure of the present life and its toil. In the Gospel: “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights.”
The Passover: the foretelling of the Lord’s passing over. In the Gospel: “Before the festival day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.”
The fifty days: the manifestation of future blessedness or of forgiveness. In Leviticus: “You shall therefore count seven full weeks, up to the following day,” and further on, that is, fifty days.
The Jubilee: a sign of the rest to come. In Leviticus: “It is a year of release; it shall be a holy sign for you.”
The city of God: the Church, or the soul. In the Psalm: “In the city of our God.”

Citizens: the faithful. In the Apostle: “But you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.” Walls: the defences of divine Scripture, or the prophets, or the saints. In the Psalm: “Let the walls of Jerusalem be built.” Again, in the opposite sense: “In my God I shall leap over a wall.”
Towers: the apostles, or all who are perfect. In the Psalm: “And abundance in your towers.”

Gates: the holy Scriptures, or righteous deeds, or the apostles, or the angels. In the Psalm: “And be lifted up, you everlasting gates.” Again, in the opposite sense: “For wide is the gate and broad the way that leads to night [?].”
Streets: the wide-open blessedness of the saints. In the Apocalypse: “And the streets of the city were pure gold, like transparent glass.”
The foundation: Christ, or faith. In the Apostle: “For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid, Christ Jesus.”
The hedge: the law, or the guardianship of angels. In the song of Isaiah: “And I put a hedge around it, and set up canes, and planted a vineyard.”
The house: the soul in which Christ dwells, or the Church. In the Psalm: “We will go into the house of the Lord.”
The upper room: the loftiness of merits or of knowledge. In the Gospel: “And he will show you a large upper room.”
Doors: the opening of faith. In the Apostle: “For a great and clear door has been opened to me.”
A pillar: spiritual support or steadfastness. In the Apostle: “James and John and Cephas, who seemed to be pillars.”
A wall: sometimes the structure of good works. In the Song of Songs: “Look, he stands here behind our wall, gazing through the windows.”
Windows: sight, or the other senses. As above: “gazing through the windows.” Again, in a bad sense: “Death will come in through your windows.”
Steps: spiritual ascent. In the title of the Psalms: “A song of steps.”
The pavement: the humbling or affliction of the soul, or its sinking toward earthly things. In the Psalm: “My soul has clung to the pavement.”
The psaltery: good works. In the Psalm: “The pleasant psaltery with the lyre.”

The lyre: the devout heart, in which the virtues, that is, spiritual goods, are like strings. In the Psalm: “Awake, psaltery and lyre”; that is, works together with faith; or, said of the Lord himself, the resurrection of the flesh together with divine power.

The ten-stringed instrument: the ten commandments, or the five senses of the outer man paired with those of the inner man. In the Psalm: “On the ten-stringed instrument, on the psaltery with song and lyre.”
The organ: man, or the man who was assumed by the Lord. In the Psalm: “Praise him with strings and organ.”
The drum: the body made lean by fasting. In the Psalm: “Praise him with drum and dance.”
The dance: harmony. In the Psalm, as above.
The trumpet: the lifting up of the voice in divine preaching. In the Prophet: “Lift up your voice like a trumpet.”
Cymbals: lips that confess God, or love of God and love of neighbour. In the Psalm: “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals.”
Jubilation: a cry poured out more fully in spiritual fervour. In the Psalm: “Praise him with cymbals of jubilation.”
Egypt: the world, or the Gentile peoples. In the Psalm: “Envoys will come out of Egypt.”

Ethiopia: the Church drawn from the Gentiles. In the Psalm: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands.” Again, in the opposite sense, in the Psalm: “You gave him as food to the people of the Ethiopians.”
Babylon: either the world or Rome. In the Apocalypse: “And great Babylon came to remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.”
Enemies: the devil, or the vices. In the Psalm: “He will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.”
Thieves: heretics, or false prophets. In the Gospel: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers.”

The nations: the vices. In the Pentateuch: “When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has destroyed many nations before you.” Again, in the opposite sense: “Clap your hands, all you nations.”
The fight: the struggle against spiritual wickedness, or the conflict against vices. In the Apostle: “So I fight, not as one beating the air.”
Peace: the harmony of flesh and spirit in what is good. In the Psalm: “Pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem.” Peace is also Christ. In the Apostle: “For he himself is our peace.”
Victory: triumph over the devil or over adversity. In the Apostle: “But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
The prize: the reward of merits brought to completion. In the Apostle: “I press on toward the goal, toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling.”
The crown: the reward of eternal glory given for righteousness. In the Apostle: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness.”

Since the completion of spiritual progress carries one forward to the crown, it is fitting that the crown should also complete this spiritual interpretation of these names. We judged it too hard a task, however, to include all such names, just as it would be to set out all those which extend into both senses with a twofold meaning.
X. ON NUMBERS
Now that these names are finished, let us also briefly set out the numbers which the mystical meaning of the examples makes the more celebrated among the sacred ones.
1: this number refers to the unity of the Godhead. In the Pentateuch: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God.”
2: to the two Testaments. In Kings: “And he made in
the inner sanctuary two cherubim, ten cubits in size.”
3: to the Trinity. In the Epistle of John: “There are three that bear witness: the water, the blood and the Spirit.”
4: to the four Gospels. In Ezekiel: “And from the midst of it the likeness of four living creatures.”
5: to the five books of Moses. The Apostle: “In the church I would rather speak five words with my mind.”

6: to the sixth day, on which the Lord made man together with all the living creatures of the earth. In Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness”; and again a little later: “And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.”
7: to the seventh day, on which God rested once all things were completed. In Genesis: “And he rested on the seventh day from all the work he had done.”
8: to the Lord’s day of the resurrection, that is, the eighth. In the title of a Psalm: “To the end, for the eighth.”
9: to the mystery that the Lord gave up his spirit at the ninth hour. In the Gospel: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice.”
10: to the Decalogue. In the Psalm: “On the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.”
12: to the apostles. In the Gospel: “Now these are the names of the twelve apostles.”
14: to the mystery of the Lord’s genealogy. In the Gospel: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations.”
15: to the fifteen steps of the Temple.
16: to the number of the prophets.
22: to the mystery of the divine books, according to the letters of the Hebrews.
24: to the mystery of the number of the elders. In the Apocalypse: “And on the thrones twenty-four elders seated.”
30: to the fruit of faithful marriages. In the Gospel: “And they will bear fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.”

33: to the mystery of the age the Lord lived to in the flesh. In the Apostle, as some take this passage: “until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to the perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.”
40: to the mystery of the forty days. In the Gospel: “And he was led by the Spirit in the desert for forty days.”
42: to the number of the stopping-places in the desert, or to the number of generations from Abraham to the Lord [?] Christ.
50: to Pentecost. In the Acts of the Apostles: “And when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled.”
60: to the fruit owed to widows or to the continent. In the Gospel: “And they will bear fruit, some sixtyfold.”

72: to the number of Moses’ elders, or of the disciples whom the Lord chose. In the Gospel: “After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others as well, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every town.”
100: to the fruit of martyrs or of virgins. In the Gospel: “And they will bear fruit, some a hundredfold.”

We have put forward these fixed and sacred numbers only by way of example. Besides these there are a great many others, indeed almost all are sacred; and you yourself, as you search the divine readings, will discover how they come to be so.
